summary:
Cabo Verde does not criminalise same-sex relations. The national employment discrimination prohibition covers sexual orientation but does not extend to gender identity, so a trans worker has no explicit statutory basis for a workplace complaint (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026).

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. In 2016 civil law blocked Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed trans woman in the country, from changing her legal name to a female one; the source inventory holds no later statute or administrative procedure permitting a legal gender change. A trans visitor whose passport marker differs from their presentation should therefore expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility.

Same-sex unions are not recognised. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva said on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, a statement made after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Trans-specific violence is documented at a personal level. Tchinda Andrade, who came out publicly in 1997 at the age of 19, reported verbal violence and two physical attacks while describing Cabo Verde as markedly freer for LGBT people than other African countries and the island of São Vicente as relaxed.

Public visibility is high and organised. LGBTIQ organisations register freely, the first public Pride was held in 2013, making Cabo Verde the second African country to do so, and the 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with NGO campaigns by the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law, with the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged in the programme.

Survey evidence points to broad public acceptance of LGBT people alongside a narrower margin on gender variance. Polling across 2019–21 found 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, and Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020) placed Cabo Verde among the particularly tolerant countries in Africa while recording that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

The state presents itself internationally as a protector: Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group and made anti-discrimination commitments under the 2024 Universal Periodic Review.
tangentialFactors:
Comparative framing in the sources consistently sets Cabo Verde apart from its continental peers. Afrobarometer's May 2020 dispatch identifies Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe as the standout tolerant countries in Africa, while noting that acceptance drops sharply on questions of sexual difference across the wider region.

The country's international positioning reinforces that divergence: it is one of only two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group, and it tabled anti-discrimination commitments in its 2024 Universal Periodic Review.

Civic advocacy has been continuous rather than episodic. Pride has run since 2013, the second African edition of the event, and the 2018 Pride Week in Praia paired a parade with a formal petition to the National Assembly, backed in public by the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women.

Political opinion at the top has been restrained rather than hostile. In July 2017 the prime minister kept same-sex marriage off the agenda while publicly distancing himself from the opposition to it voiced by MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro.

On the ground, the country's most prominent trans woman rated São Vicente as relaxed even while recording two physical assaults and repeated verbal abuse, suggesting that tolerance measured in surveys does not eliminate targeted violence against visibly trans people.
localsOnly:
Resident workers are protected against workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation under national employment law, but gender identity is not a listed ground, so trans employees must argue their cases without a dedicated statutory hook.

Legal gender change is unavailable. Civil law refused Tchinda Andrade's request to register a female name in 2016, and no subsequent statute or administrative route appears in the sources.

Marriage and civil union recognition for same-sex couples does not exist, and the prime minister's July 2017 statement placed the question outside government planning after community demands for civil unions and marriage.

LGBTIQ associations operate openly: they register without hindrance, three of them campaigned during the 2018 Pride Week in Praia, and the National Assembly has received their petitions for marriage equality and a comprehensive anti-discrimination law.

Public attitudes measured in 2019–21 show 82% of respondents would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, though Afrobarometer's 2020 regional work finds that acceptance of sexual minorities stays weak among younger age groups.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory contains no source dated after 2016 on legal gender recognition, so whether any administrative procedure for changing a legal gender has since been introduced is not established either way.

Unresolved: the 2018 petition to the National Assembly for an anti-discrimination law is documented, but no source states whether such a law was subsequently enacted, and the current coverage beyond the employment-law sexual-orientation ground is unconfirmed.

Not sourced: the dossier has no material on hate-crime sentencing enhancements, on public-order or decency provisions that might be applied to trans people, or on their enforcement.

Not sourced: no entry, visa or border-screening rules are available, including whether passport gender markers are checked or whether trans travellers face additional questioning.

Not sourced: access to gender-affirming healthcare, locker-room and bathroom access rules, and school or institutional facility policies are absent from the inventory.

The public-opinion figures date from 2019–21 and May 2020 and have not been refreshed by the sources; they may not reflect current attitudes.
